# OpenBrief: scenario authoring guide for LLMs

OpenBrief (https://noahdemar.github.io/conflict-sandbox/) is a browser tool
that turns map scenarios of real events into illustrated articles: prose with
embedded map scenes (units moving on real roads, strikes, lighting by real sun
position, a scripted camera) and image callouts. Articles can be embedded in
other websites.

A scenario is a single JSON document. To make one, produce JSON that validates
against the schema, then load it in the app (see "Loading" below).

- JSON Schema: https://noahdemar.github.io/conflict-sandbox/schema/scenario.schema.json
- Content packs by period: https://noahdemar.github.io/conflict-sandbox/packs/index.json
- Complete, valid examples (study the closest one before writing):
  - https://noahdemar.github.io/conflict-sandbox/examples/river-crossing.json: minimal hypothetical battle, written out longhand
  - https://noahdemar.github.io/conflict-sandbox/examples/authored-river-crossing.json: the same battle written with the shortcuts (named places, relative times, a macro, story beats, automatic camera)
  - https://noahdemar.github.io/conflict-sandbox/examples/khasham.json: modern battle with air strikes, article, callouts, order of battle
  - https://noahdemar.github.io/conflict-sandbox/examples/binladen-raid.json: raid with individual people, helicopters, night vision, satellite pass
  - https://noahdemar.github.io/conflict-sandbox/examples/dogfight.json: 3D aerial scene over real terrain with an aircraft comparison
  - https://noahdemar.github.io/conflict-sandbox/examples/index.json: machine-readable list of all examples

Output ONLY the JSON document when asked for a scenario: no prose, no comments,
no trailing commas.

## Agentic authoring loop (browser access)

If you are an AI assistant that can drive a browser (Claude Code, Codex CLI,
Gemini CLI, Cursor, Windsurf/Devin, VS Code Copilot agent mode), do not just
emit JSON and hope — the published site validates and plays any fetchable
scenario. No repository or install needed:

1. Write the scenario JSON, then open
   `https://noahdemar.github.io/conflict-sandbox/?scenario=<url>` where <url>
   is anywhere the file can be fetched:
   - quickest: `gh gist create scenario.json --public` and use the raw file
     URL, or any static host that allows cross-origin fetches;
   - no hosting: append `encodeURIComponent("data:application/json;base64," +
     base64(file))` after `?scenario=` and open that (fine for typical
     scenario sizes; prefer a hosted URL for very large documents).
2. The page resolves and validates before it plays: schema errors, reference
   errors, plausibility warnings and composition findings are listed on screen
   and in the browser console. The whole report is also left on
   `window.__openbriefReport`, so you can read it directly:
   `await page.evaluate(() => window.__openbriefReport)` returns
   `{ ok, errors, notes, issues: [{ path, message, severity, fix }] }`.
   Fix the JSON and reload until it comes back ok.
3. With the repository, the same check runs without a browser, and draws a
   storyboard you can look at in one image instead of scrubbing the film:
       npm run check -- scenario.json
       npm run check -- scenario.json --json
       npm run check -- scenario.json --storyboard sb.svg --resolved plain.json
   `--resolved` writes the plain scenario the shortcuts expanded into: read it
   to see exactly where things were placed and when they happen.
4. Watch the timeline for what a still cannot show: unit spacing, effect
   timing, how the camera moves. Iterate until it looks right.
5. Deliver the JSON plus the preview URL.

If you have no tools, tell the user this workflow exists and produces much
better results — then still return valid JSON.

## Top-level shape

Use the exported file wrapper (recommended):

{
  "format": "conflict-sandbox-scenario",
  "version": 1,
  "duration": 60,                // timeline length in seconds
  "roster": [ ...RosterEntry ],  // optional; gives units better silhouettes
  "scenario": { ...Scenario }
}

A bare Scenario object is also accepted.

Scenario keys: name, subtitle (place and date line for the opening title
card), sources (list of references for the closing card), factions, units, arrows, territories, labels, strikes,
keyframes (all required arrays except name), plus optional effects,
environment, duration, period.

## Shortcuts: write less, get more (recommended)

Everything under this heading is optional sugar. The app resolves it into an
ordinary scenario before anything plays, so what you deliver stays editable by
hand and the schema still applies. Use it: hand-computing coordinates and
timings is where scenarios go wrong.

Anchor the geography once, then hang everything off it:

  "places": { "Bridge": [35.045, 48.446], "Ridge": [35.052, 48.452] }   // [lng, lat]

  { "id": "u_def", "at": "Ridge", ... }
  { "id": "u_heli", "near": { "of": "Bridge", "bearingDeg": 45, "km": 6 }, ... }
  { "id": "a_route", "via": ["Staging area", { "of": "Bridge", "bearingDeg": 200, "km": 1.2 }, "Bridge"] }

`at` and `near.of` accept a name from `places` or the id of anything already
placed: a unit, a label, a strike, "a_route" for the first point of a route,
"a_route.end" for its last. `via` replaces `points` on arrows and
territories. Anything given lat/lng directly still works.

TIMES may be expressions instead of numbers:

  "start"        0
  "end"          the end of the timeline (needs an explicit duration)
  "u_heli"       when that object starts: appearAt / time / start
  "a_route.end"  when it ends: route end, effect end
  "s_hit"        when a strike LANDS (impact, not launch)
  "s_hit-4"      four seconds before it lands; "+2" works the same way

So "launchAt": "s_hit-8" is an eight-second flight, and
"destroyedAt": "s_hit" kills the target exactly when the strike arrives.
Change one time and everything hanging off it moves with it.

MACROS expand into ordinary units, routes and strikes:

  { "macro": "column", "id": "m_adv", "factionId": "f_red", "count": 6,
    "via": ["Staging area", "Objective"], "startAt": 4, "duration": 24,
    "unit": { "name": "T-72", "type": "armor", "icon": "tank" } }
    -> one route plus six vehicles queued on it (the app spaces them out)

  { "macro": "formation", "id": "m_line", "factionId": "f_blue", "count": 5,
    "center": "Ridge", "shape": "line", "facingDeg": 180, "frontageM": 900,
    "unit": { "name": "Longbowmen", "type": "infantry", "icon": "archers" } }
    shapes: line | wedge | block | column | shieldwall

  { "macro": "strike-package", "id": "m_fires", "from": "u_f15e",
    "targets": ["u_t72_1", "u_t72_2"], "weapon": "GBU-38 JDAM",
    "at": 42, "intervalSeconds": 2.5 }
    targets may be unit ids, place names or [lng, lat]; a unit target becomes
    targetUnitId, so the impact follows a moving vehicle

  { "macro": "volley", "id": "m_arrows", "from": "u_archers",
    "target": "u_vanguard", "at": 20, "count": 4, "rounds": 14 }
    pre-modern massed ranged fire: repeated many-round volleys

Macro output ids are "<macro id>_1", "<macro id>_2" and so on, and the route
is "<macro id>_route", so strikes, beats and keyframes can reference them.

THE CAMERA can compose itself. Write story beats and set
"keyframes": "auto":

  "keyframes": "auto",
  "beats": [
    { "at": 0, "caption": "A Red armoured column moves on the bridge at dawn.",
      "shot": "establish", "focus": ["m_adv_1", "u_def", "l_bridge"] },
    { "at": "s_hit-7", "caption": "An Apache runs in from the north east.",
      "shot": "action", "focus": ["u_heli", "m_adv_1"] },
    { "caption": "The crossing is held.", "shot": "aftermath",
      "focus": ["u_def", "l_bridge"] }
  ]

Each beat becomes a shot framed on the ids in `focus` at that moment, tilted
and zoomed to suit `shot` (establish | approach | action | detail |
aftermath), long enough for the caption to be read aloud, tracking a single
moving subject automatically. A beat without `at` follows the previous one at
reading pace. Optional per beat: follow, hold, sensor, overlay,
overlayFactionIds, narrate, media.

Write keyframes by hand when you want exact control, and you can still leave
work to the app: a keyframe with a caption and highlightUnitIds but no
lng/lat/zoom is framed for you, and "at": "Bridge" centres it on a place.

With no beats and no keyframes, "keyframes": "auto" composes a shot list from
the events themselves and writes placeholder captions. Rewrite those captions.

CONTENT PACKS carry period rosters and are pulled in at the top level:

  "include": ["modern/nato", "modern/opfor"]

then point units at them with "rosterId": "mod_abrams". The packs are listed
at https://noahdemar.github.io/conflict-sandbox/packs/index.json and each one
is published at .../packs/<id>.json. A period includes its own packs
automatically.

## Conventions that matter

- TIME is timeline seconds from 0 to `duration`. Every event has a time
  (appearAt, destroyedAt, launchAt, start, keyframe time...). Keep all times
  within the duration.
- COORDINATE ORDER: `points` arrays are [longitude, latitude]. Units and
  labels use separate `lat` and `lng` fields. Do not swap them.
- IDS must be unique within their list; references (factionId, arrowId,
  fromUnitId, targetUnitId, unitId, targetUnitId, followUnitId, rosterId)
  must point at existing ids.
- Keep each camera shot (gap between keyframes) at least as long as its caption
  takes to read aloud: roughly 1 second per 2.5 words, plus half a second.
- Captions are read aloud by text-to-speech, so write them to be spoken:
  spell initialisms with spaced letters ("U S", "E K I A") or use full names; no bracketed
  asides, no abbreviations like "approx.", "e.g.", "vs.", "km" (spell them
  out), no "~", "/" or "&". Prefer plain words over symbols and write
  numbers the way you'd say them. The app normalizes common cases, but
  clean text sounds best.
- Be factual for real events and mark anything invented or approximate in the
  caption or name, e.g. "approximately", "Illustrative:", "Hypothetical:".

## Periods: the content is split by era

Set "period" on the scenario. It selects the icons, unit packs and rules that
belong together, and decides the visual treatment, so era never has to be
thought about separately:

  ancient      to about 500 AD        phalanx, legion, chariots, galleys
  medieval     about 500 to 1500      men-at-arms, longbows, knights, siege
  gunpowder    about 1500 to 1800     pike and shot, field cannon, sail
  industrial   about 1800 to 1913     rifle regiments, massed batteries, rail
  ww1          1914 to 1918           trenches, barrages, first tanks
  ww2          1939 to 1945           armour, half-tracks, piston aircraft
  coldwar      1946 to 1991           jets, helicopters, missile air defence
  modern       1991 onwards           precision fires, drones, satellites

The first four use the historical look: an aged palette with modern roads,
buildings, borders and place names hidden, and no automatic road routing.
"era": "historical" or "modern" still works and overrides the default.

Rules that come with the period (the check reports icons out of place):

- Pre-modern: name formations, not head counts, such as "Longbowmen",
  "Dismounted men-at-arms", "Mounted knights", "Royal standard" or "Baggage
  train". Name strikes "Longbow volley", "Melee", "Cavalry charge", "Musket
  volley" or "Cannonade". A group icon is a formation, not a literal head
  count. No modern communications or weapons; "Demolition charges" remain
  explosive, not melee.
- ww1: trench systems are territories, the attack is arrows across no
  man’s land, a barrage is a salvo. Aircraft observe and fight each other;
  they carry nothing guided.
- ww2: halftrack, propfighter, propbomber, higgins, uboat. No jets,
  helicopters, drones, satellites or guided weapons. Bomb sticks and strafing
  runs use pattern "line".
- coldwar: mostly unguided fires; air defence is a real constraint
  (airDefenseKm). No armed drones and no live imagery feeds.
- modern: precision weapons need explicit launchAt and targetUnitId; show the
  sensing as well as the shooting.

## Factions

{ "id": "f_blue", "name": "Blue", "color": "#3a6fc0", "affiliation": "friend" }

affiliation: friend | hostile | neutral | unknown. It sets military symbol frame
shape, air-defense targeting and thermal colouring (hostiles glow red).

## Units

Required: id, factionId, type, name, lat, lng, appearAt.
type: infantry | armor | artillery | air | naval | missile | hq.

Icons: set "icon" on every unit (or on its roster entry) to a key from the
shared icon library below. Pick the closest match. If nothing fits, name what
you wanted anyway: OpenBrief shows a generic icon for the unit type and the
importer lists every unknown icon so it can be fixed. Common synonyms also work
("destroyer" draws "ship", "trebuchet" draws "siege", "humvee" draws "jeep").

People: soldier, troops, officer, medic, sniper, civilians, dog
Ground vehicles: tank, abrams, bradley, halftrack, ifv, apc, jeep, truck, motorcycle, ambulance, tanker, engineer, howitzer, spg, mortar, launcher, sam, aagun, radar
Aircraft: jet, f15, f22, bomber, flyingwing, transport, gunship, airliner, heli, attackheli, mi8, drone, cruisemissile, satellite, propfighter, propbomber, proptransport
Ships: ship, carrier, submarine, uboat, patrolboat, landingcraft, higgins, lcac, cargoship
Structures: hq, bunker, checkpoint, camp, fort
Pre-modern: menatarms, spearmen, pikemen, archers, musketeers, cavalry, chariot, cannon, siege, banner, baggage, sailingship, galley

Without "icon", the icon is guessed from the unit name, so still name things
concretely: "T-72", "BMP-1", "D-30 howitzer", "HIMARS", "F-15E", "AH-64",
"MQ-9 Reaper", "B-52", "Chinook", "Operator 1-1" (a single person),
"English longbowmen", "Mounted knights".

Optional:
- heading (degrees), arrowId (follow a route), destroyedAt, leavesAt (removed
  from the scene, e.g. boarding), rangeKm (range ring)
- sensorKm: terrain-aware line-of-sight area for ground units
- airDefenseKm: engagement envelope that turns red when enemy aircraft enter
- landAtEnd (aircraft set down at route end instead of loitering)
- altitudeKm + orbitRole "relay" | "imaging" (+ captureAt for an imaging
  pass): renders a satellite in 3D above its ground track. Altitude must be
  over 100 km (the edge of space) and is typically 500+ km for imaging
  satellites. Every non-geostationary satellite MOVES: give it an arrowId
  route. Only a geostationary satellite (altitudeKm about 35786) may hold
  position.

Aircraft without landAtEnd circle over the end of their route. Ground vehicles
sharing one route queue, drive in column and halt in line automatically; they
pull away and brake smoothly and slow down on uphill stretches.

## Arrows (routes)

Required: id, factionId, points ([lng, lat] list), name, appearAt, duration
(seconds to traverse). A unit follows a route by `arrowId`.

- Ground units snap to real roads by default (followRoads: false to disable).
- hideLine: true = move along the path without drawing an arrow (good for
  individual people).
- times: one absolute time per point for precise pacing with holds
  (repeat a point with a later time to wait there). Overrides duration pacing.
- hideAt: stop drawing the arrow after this time.

## Strikes

Required: id, lat, lng, name, size (0.1 small arms … 1.5 large bomb), appearAt
(impact time).

The visual is chosen from `name`:
- guns: "30mm", "chain gun", "cannon", "rifle", "small arms" → tracers, sparks
- bombs: "JDAM", "GBU", "Mk 82", "bomb" → dropped, brief flash, dirt and dust
  (from an air unit the bomb falls below the release point in an accelerating
  drop, not a rising missile arc; give it a fromUnitId and a short flight time)
- shells: "howitzer", "105mm", "mortar", "fire mission" → arcing round, dirt
- anything else → missile/rocket with motor glow and smoke trail

Optional: fromUnitId + launchAt (fly from that unit; without launchAt the
flight time is derived from weapon type and distance), targetUnitId (impact
follows that unit's position at impact time; use this for moving targets),
salvo + spreadM (multiple rounds), targetStrikeId (interceptor),
impactStyle: "blast" (default) or "fireball" (explicit fuel-rich treatment),
pattern: "disc" or "line" (salvo spread shape).

Salvo patterns: "disc" scatters rounds around the aim point (artillery sheaf —
the default for ground weapons). "line" walks them along the attack axis from
fromUnitId toward the aim point in firing order — use it for strafing runs
("Strafing run", "30mm gun run"), bomb sticks and rocket ripples. Gun, bomb
and missile salvos launched by an AIR unit get "line" automatically; set
pattern: "disc" to opt out. spreadM is the disc radius or the line half-length
in meters; a strafe over 60 to 120 meters reads well.

Use "blast" for normal high-explosive impacts. A large weapon is not automatically
a fuel explosion: only choose "fireball" when the target/event supports it.
Gun, arrow and melee impacts remain non-fireball effects regardless of this option.
`size` is an illustrative visual scale, NOT explosive yield or casualty radius.
For rifle shots start around 0.04 to 0.12 with spreadM: 1 to 3; use small bursts,
not a continuous stream. The editor permits scales down to 0.02 and exposes scatter.
A salvo must contain 1 to 256 rounds. Prefer several well-timed small bursts over
hundreds of simultaneous effects; count them as illustrative fire, not a literal
reconstruction of every round fired. The first round uses the exact authored
launchAt and appearAt; later rounds follow with deterministic cadence and scatter.

Pair a destroyed unit's destroyedAt with the impact time of the strike that
hits it.

Realism: keep shooters within real weapon reach (e.g. Grad about 20 km,
122mm/155mm howitzers 15 to 30 km, GMLRS about 85 km, Hellfire about 11 km,
30mm cannon about 4 km, small arms under 1 km). Give munitions flight time
that grows with distance, and don't fire from units before they appear or
after they are destroyed. Timelines may compress time, but keep ground moves
within a couple hundred times real vehicle speed. The importer lists any
violations.

## Status effects (`effects`)

{ "id": "fx1", "kind": "radio", "unitId": "u_def", "start": 8, "duration": 4, "label": "CALLING FIRES" }

kind: radio | datalink (needs targetUnitId) | jamming (radiusM) | panic |
wounded (crippled, smoking) | noammo.

## Territories and labels

Territory: id, factionId, points ([lng, lat] ring), name, appearAt, duration
(fade-in). Optional `label` draws large faint text across it.

Label: id, text, lat, lng, size, color, appearAt. Optional `flag` (ISO country
code, e.g. "us") or `facility`: oil | gas | refinery | airbase | port | power |
base | hq | bridge | hospital | town.

## Camera, captions and sensor views (`keyframes`)

{ "id": "k1", "time": 0, "lng": 35.05, "lat": 48.45, "zoom": 12, "pitch": 0,
  "bearing": 0, "caption": "Opening line" }

- zoom: ~4 region, ~9 city, ~13 neighbourhood, ~17–19 individual buildings.
- pitch 0 = top-down; 45–65 for cinematic angles.
- followUnitId + followMode "track" keeps a unit centred; "chase" aligns with
  its heading. orbitSpeed rotates in degrees per timeline second; use sparingly.
- highlightUnitIds: ["u1", "u2"] adds subtle faction-colored highlights. Mention
  those units clearly in the caption; avoid highlighting every unit at once.
- overlay: "orbat" shows the hierarchical order of battle; overlayFactionIds
  optionally limits it to particular factions. Destroyed units gray out live.
- sensor: "nvg" (night vision) or "thermal" for that shot. Omit by default;
  these are illustrative filters, not evidence of actual recorded imagery.
- media: { src, caption, credit, anchor: [lng, lat], anchorRadiusM } shows an
  image beside a site (src must be a URL the site can load).
- Captions play as recorded narration when the scenario ships recordings;
  narrate: false makes a line text-only.

## Environment (optional)

{ "startHour": 21.5, "endHour": 5.9, "date": "2018-02-07", "utcOffset": 3,
  "windDirDeg": 65, "windKph": 14, "haze": 0.15,
  "cloudCover": 0.3, "precipitation": "none", "precipIntensity": 0.5 }

Lighting follows the real sun for that date, time and place (night, dawn,
twilight bands at world scale). endHour may be less than startHour to cross
midnight. hourKeys: [[seconds, localHours], …] makes the clock jump (hours may
exceed 24, e.g. a cut to the next morning). Wind steers smoke, rain, snow and
dust. cloudCover (0..1) flattens the light; precipitation is none | rain |
snow | dust. Use the real weather for real events when known.

## Article (`article`, optional)

View links and embeds open an article: headline (from `name`), standfirst
(`subtitle`), prose, map scenes, callouts and `sources`. Without `article`,
one is generated from the captions. Blocks, in reading order:

{ "kind": "heading", "text": "The column moves" }
{ "kind": "text", "text": "A paragraph of prose." }
{ "kind": "scene", "from": "k3", "to": "k4", "caption": "Short figure caption" }
  plays from keyframe k3 up to the keyframe after k4, then holds
{ "kind": "callout", "title": "T-72 tank", "text": "One or two sentences.",
  "wikiTitle": "T-72", "side": "left" }
  image comes from that Wikipedia article (or give "image": URL + "credit")
{ "kind": "image", "src": "https://...", "caption": "...", "credit": "..." }

Write the prose like a news explainer: plain, factual, attributed where
claims are disputed. Keep callouts to a few per article.

## 3D aerial scenes (`aerial`, optional)

For air combat. Keyframes that set `aerial` switch from the map to a 3D view
with aircraft built into the app (no model files). Everything else (captions,
article scenes, sources) works as usual.

"aerial": {
  "origin": [106.262, 21.395],          // [lng, lat] of the local frame
  "style": "cinematic",                 // or "briefing" (viewers can switch)
  "terrain": "real",                    // real elevation around origin; or jungle | desert | sea | plain
  "terrainTexture": "basemap",          // name-free map; "satellite" shows today's landscape
  "terrainRadiusKm": 30,
  "aircraft": [
    { "id": "f4", "name": "F-4C", "factionId": "f_usaf", "airframe": "f4",
      "track": [[0, 300, -8000, 4200], [1, 300, -7770, 4195], ...],
      "destroyedAt": 72 }
  ],
  "weapons": [
    { "id": "w1", "kind": "guns", "from": "mig", "target": "f4", "time": 40, "duration": 1.2 },
    { "id": "w2", "kind": "missile", "from": "f4", "target": "mig", "time": 68, "duration": 2.8 }
  ],
  "holds": [{ "at": 21, "seconds": 12 }]
}

- airframe: f4 | mig17 | jet (generic).
- track points are [flight seconds, meters east, meters north, meters
  altitude] from origin. Sample every 0.5 to 1 s through maneuvers; bank and
  pitch are computed from the curve, so keep speeds realistic and turns smooth
  (no instant changes of speed or direction). Real terrain uses real ground
  height, so keep altitudes well above the hills.
- Aircraft and weapon times are flight seconds. `holds` freeze the aircraft
  (not the camera) for explanation: at timeline second `at`, flight time stops
  for `seconds`. Keyframe times stay in timeline seconds.
- Guns only look and sound right at gun range: put the shooter within about
  300 to 600 m behind or beside the target when firing.
- destroyedAt: the aircraft falls trailing smoke from that flight time; pair
  it with a missile impact (time + duration).

Keyframe camera shots: { "aerial": { "mode": "...", "target": "f4", ... } }
- chase: behind the target (distanceM default about 4.5 aircraft lengths)
- side: beside it
- flyby: a fixed camera the target passes about 3 s into the shot
- overview: orbits above target (and secondary); set distanceM so both fill
  the frame (usually 300 to 1500 m; far shots make aircraft hard to see)
- compare: target and secondary side by side on turntables with a stats
  panel. Pair it with a hold so the fight waits:
  "compare": { "rows": [ { "label": "Top speed", "values": ["Mach 2.2", "1,150 km/h"], "bars": [2370, 1150] } ],
               "note": "Approximate published figures." }
  Use real, widely published figures and mark them approximate.

Label the scene as an illustrative reconstruction unless the flight paths
come from real data.

## Narration

Voice is pre-recorded only (the site's demos ship recordings). Captions
without a recording are shown as text; nothing is synthesized for viewers.

## Quality checklist before delivery

1. Establish geography and chronology first. Cite verifiable sources; distinguish
   confirmed events from disputed accounts, inferred positions and illustrative
   weapon-to-target assignments. Never invent radio links, electronic jamming,
   exact casualties or sensor footage just to make a scene more dramatic.
2. Compose an establishing view, an approach, the central event, and an aftermath.
   Keep the subject visible before launch and through impact. Avoid large zoom
   changes and abrupt switches into/out of a tracking shot during the event.
   Use one principal subject per shot, with space for captions and the ORBAT card.
3. For aircraft, put every release inside the authored route window; use explicit
   launchAt and targetUnitId for moving shooters/targets. Keep helicopter approach
   speeds decreasing and repeat the landing position at later waypoint times for
   a hover. Do not duplicate waypoint TIMES or teleport onto the landing point.
4. Reserve enough time for every salvo's last round and every narration line.
   Estimate speech at about 2.5 words per second, then measure the actual recording
   and leave at least 0.5 seconds of slack. Regenerate changed captions with
   `npm run narration -- <demo-id>`; FFMPEG_PATH may select the local encoder.
   Do not generate voice live during a performance-sensitive playback or recording.
5. Article scenes deliberately hold at their end: group continuous action in one
   scene, and end between events rather than during a volley or spoken sentence.
   Backgrounding the tab pauses playback to avoid skipping action on return.
6. Use small particle scales and restrained highlights. Keep only meaningful
   status effects and avoid overlapping large smoke plumes. Reuse movement routes
   and aggregate formations when individual people are not essential to the story.
7. Run `npm run check -- scenario.json` (schema, references, event times,
   plausibility and composition, with a storyboard), plus `npm run build` and
   `npm test` in the repository. Plausibility warnings are heuristics, not
   historical certification. Review every finding rather than treating a
   schema-valid result as approval.
8. Preview at normal and double speed, scrub both directions, pause during audio,
   switch scenes, and check a narrow viewport. Listen for overlapping narration,
   delayed effects and excessive loudness. Check browser frame timings on target
   hardware; automated tests alone cannot establish cinematic quality or frame rate.

## Loading

1. In the editor: Import → paste JSON (resolved and validated with exact error
   messages) or choose a .json file. After loading, the editor walks through
   every finding one at a time, selecting the object it is about.
2. By URL: https://noahdemar.github.io/conflict-sandbox/?scenario=<URL of a
   publicly readable JSON file that allows cross-origin requests>
   (e.g. a GitHub Gist "raw" link).
3. Remix a finished example in the editor:
   https://noahdemar.github.io/conflict-sandbox/?remix=khasham
   (also binladen-raid, dogfight, agincourt), or Create a Brief → Remix.
